incident_summary: Ben Black, the 40-year-old son of Apollo Global Management co-founder Leon Black, was appointed by Trump to lead the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), a federal agency overseeing $205 billion in taxpayer-backed international investments, and was sworn in at a White House ceremony. Justice Department records and a Guardian review of more than 5,000 pages of Jeffrey Epstein's private correspondence found that Ben Black invested in the same company as Epstein in 2011 and maintained a personal and business relationship with him for several years afterward, including shared investments and direct communications. A spokesperson for Ben Black stated: 'Ben Black had no personal or professional relationship with Jeffrey Epstein,' a denial that directly contradicts the documentary evidence in the DOJ records and Guardian's review of Epstein's own correspondence.

incident_summary: DOJ has pursued two separate grand jury investigations (Southern District of Florida, opened November 2025 and January 2026) into former CIA Director John Brennan's role in the intelligence community's 2016 assessment that Russia sought to help Donald Trump's presidential campaign. AP reporting (Feb. 17, 2026) confirmed DOJ expanded the same Florida-based investigation with a new wave of subpoenas targeting additional former FBI officials Peter Strzok and Lisa Page over their roles in the 2016-2017 Russia intelligence assessment -- alongside DOJ's separately-documented subpoena of former FBI Director James Comey over the same assessment (see halligan-comey-vindictive-prosecution-2025-2026.json). Brennan's lawyers said they had been told he is a target but had not been told of any 'legally justifiable basis for undertaking this investigation.' CBS News reported that by March 20, 2026, federal prosecutors had issued more than 130 subpoenas since the investigation began, expanding it to also target former FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe alongside Brennan, Strzok, and Page, and had again subpoenaed James Comey (whose separate earlier indictment was dismissed in November 2025; see halligan-comey-vindictive-prosecution-2025-2026.json) as part of this broader probe. Prosecutors are pursuing a theory that Obama-era officials coordinated a 'grand conspiracy' against Trump beginning with the 2016 Russia assessment and continuing through the Biden-era criminal cases against him. A career prosecutor assigned to the matter raised concerns about the investigation and was removed from the case in April 2026; Joseph DiGenova -- a Trump ally, former Trump campaign lawyer, and now a counselor to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- was installed to lead the investigation in the career prosecutor's place. The grand jury is empaneled in Fort Pierce, Florida, whose only federal judge is Trump-appointed Aileen Cannon; Brennan separately asked the SDFL chief judge to block Cannon from overseeing the case, accusing DOJ of manipulating case-assignment procedures specifically to secure her as the presiding judge. Reuters reported (May 12, 2026) that the FBI began questioning current and former CIA officers as part of the DOJ investigation into Brennan's role in the 2017 intelligence assessment concluding Russia interfered in the 2016 election to help Trump -- an active investigative step examining Brennan's role and testimony despite multiple prior independent reviews having already affirmed Russia's 2016 election interference. On July 1, 2026, Brennan sued DOJ seeking a court order requiring the department to preserve records related to both investigations, laying groundwork for an anticipated vindictive/selective-prosecution defense should charges be filed.

incident_summary: DOJ proposed a rule making it easier for states to obtain certification for an accelerated federal review process for death penalty cases under a 1996 federal law (the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act's Chapter 154 opt-in provisions). official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General
offense_category: Wholesale Deprioritization of Federal Criminal Enforcement Outside Immigration -- a prosecutorial-discretion and resource-allocation accountability claim, not an allegation that declining any specific case was individually improper
incident_summary: A ProPublica investigation, examining two decades of DOJ case-declination data, found DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi closed more than 23,000 criminal investigations without prosecution in the first six months of the administration -- including cases involving terrorism, fraud, corruption, labor racketeering, drug trafficking, and environmental crimes -- while ramping up immigration prosecutions. The majority of the declined cases had been referred to DOJ by law enforcement agencies, including under prior administrations, whose investigators believed a federal crime may have been committed. February 2025 alone, covering the first weeks of Bondi's tenure, saw nearly 11,000 declinations -- the most in a single month since at least 2004, when comparable data begins, and far exceeding the prior monthly high of roughly 6,500 declinations set in September 2019 during Trump's first term. ProPublica's analysis found the increase was not attributable to a larger inherited caseload or increased referral volume from law enforcement, indicating a deliberate shift in prosecutorial priority rather than a passive resourcing effect.

The declined cases span multiple serious categories (terrorism, fraud, corruption, labor racketeering, drugs, environmental crimes), not a single narrow category
The February 2025 monthly declination total (~11,000) is the highest in at least two decades of comparable data, exceeding even the prior high recorded during Trump's first term

ProPublica's analysis ruled out caseload inheritance or referral-volume increases as explanations, supporting a characterization of the decline as a deliberate prioritization shift toward immigration enforcement

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General Jan 2025-Apr 2026 (oversaw the dismantling); Todd Blanche, Attorney General since April 2026 (acting until Senate confirmation August 8, 2026), has not restored the unit

incident_summary: Under Attorney General Pam Bondi, DOJ's Public Integrity Section -- the unit responsible for prosecuting public corruption by federal, state, and local officials -- was reduced from roughly 36-40 full-time attorneys handling 175-200 open matters at the start of the second Trump term to just two attorneys overseeing about 20 remaining investigations by May 2026, per current and former DOJ officials. The section, the oldest of its kind since its 1976 creation, has never been this small. The staffing cut coincided with parallel rollbacks elsewhere in DOJ's anti-corruption infrastructure: a pause in enforcing the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act against U.S. executives who bribe foreign officials, disbanding of an FBI squad devoted to investigating congressional misconduct, disbanding of a task force pursuing Russian oligarchs' assets, and a pullback in enforcing the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Over the same period, Trump pardoned at least 15 people who had been charged with or convicted of public corruption, including political allies and supporters. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse sent DOJ a formal oversight letter demanding answers on the section's dismantling. Bondi left DOJ in April 2026; Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal defense attorney, became acting Attorney General and has not publicly moved to restore the section's staffing.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (served 2025-2026, removed April 2026)
offense_category: DOJ Leadership Blocking Investigation of a Federal Agent's Fatal Shooting While Pressuring an Investigation of the Victim's Widow -- potential obstruction/prosecutorial-misconduct pattern, distinct from an ordinary declination decision
incident_summary: ICE agent Jonathan Ross fatally shot Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother of three, in south Minneapolis on January 7, 2026, during Operation Metro Surge; Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said video evidence did not appear to support DHS's account that Good was using her SUV to run over an agent. Rather than pursuing a standard investigation of Ross's use of deadly force, top DOJ officials pressured the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota to instead investigate Good's widow, Becca Good, reportedly examining any ties she might have to activist groups. An FBI Minneapolis field-office supervisor who attempted to investigate Ross himself was pressured to step away from that investigation and subsequently resigned. In response, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson -- the office's lead prosecutor on the high-profile Feeding Our Future fraud case, which had charged 78 people and secured 58 convictions -- resigned along with five colleagues (Harry Jacobs, Melinda Williams, Thomas Calhoun-Lopez, Ruth Schneider, and Tom Hollenhurst) in mid-January 2026, citing DOJ's reluctance to investigate the agent and the push to investigate Good's widow instead. Eight additional assistant U.S. attorneys, including civil division chief Ana Voss, left the office in early February 2026, citing continued frustration with how DOJ was handling both the Good case and the separate fatal shooting of Alex Pretti by federal agents.

incident_summary: Alina Habba, a former personal defense attorney for Trump, was installed as acting/interim U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey. A federal judge ruled her appointment unlawful, finding the arrangement violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act and, separately, that a structure allowing the administration to unilaterally extend her tenure past normal limits amounted to 'a unilateral appointment in violation of the Constitution's Appointments Clause.' An appeals court upheld the disqualification ruling, and Habba resigned in December 2025. Rather than nominating a Senate-confirmable replacement, Attorney General Bondi then appointed three individuals -- Philip Lamparello, Jordan Fox, and Ari Fontecchio -- to jointly divide the U.S. Attorney's responsibilities among themselves. A federal judge ruled this arrangement was also unlawful, finding DOJ had unlawfully split the power of the U.S. Attorney's office among the three-person team specifically to route around the earlier disqualification ruling. In the most recent escalation, the same judge (per AP News) threw a government prosecutor out of court and ordered the top officials running the New Jersey U.S. Attorney's Office to testify under oath, condemning DOJ's leadership structure there as 'chaotic' and potentially unconstitutional.

incident_summary: Abigail (Gail) Slater, Assistant Attorney General for the DOJ's Antitrust Division, was forced out in February 2026 after roughly a year leading the division, during which she pursued aggressive antitrust enforcement. Friction with the White House had been building for months: in December 2025, Trump issued a 'full and unconditional pardon' for Oak View Group co-founder Tim Leiweke, who had been indicted by Slater's own division earlier in 2025 -- undercutting an active enforcement action from within her own department. She had also lost the confidence of AG Bondi and Deputy AG Blanche, with a source telling reporters officials felt new leadership was needed to advance the President's agenda; a separate travel-rules dispute (an unauthorized trip to a Paris conference) led DOJ to cut off Slater's government credit card access. Slater suggested in a public post that she was leaving voluntarily, but CNN's sourcing characterized the departure as a firing. Bondi publicly thanked Slater for her service; DOJ named Omeed Assefi acting antitrust chief. House Judiciary Democrats sent a formal letter to Bondi regarding the Antitrust Division following Slater's departure.

offense_category: Retaliatory Firing of Career DOJ Staff Over Association with Special Counsel Jack Smith's Trump Prosecutions -- undermining internal ethics oversight and eroding a structural check (the Merit Systems Protection Board) that would ordinarily let the fired employees contest it
incident_summary: On July 11, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi fired Joseph Tirrell, the career director of DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office, in a four-sentence termination letter that gave no reason. Tirrell had spent nearly 20 years at the department and had led the ethics office since 2023, reviewing and approving financial disclosures, recusals, and conflict-of-interest waivers for DOJ leadership including Bondi herself, Deputy AG Todd Blanche, and FBI Director Kash Patel. Tirrell's portfolio had also included advising then-Special Counsel Jack Smith on ethics matters during Smith's prosecutions of Trump, including approving roughly $140,000 in free legal fees Smith received from a major Washington law firm. Tirrell was fired the same day Bondi dismissed at least 20 other DOJ employees with ties to Smith's prosecutions team, as part of a broader purge. Tirrell, along with two other fired former DOJ officials (Michael M. Gordon and Patricia A. Hartman), filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seeking immediate reinstatement and back pay. The lawsuit noted that fired federal employees would normally be able to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board, but that the board had been left without a quorum after Trump removed one of its members -- leaving the plaintiffs without the administrative appeal process Congress designed for exactly this situation.

Tirrell's own prior work included ethics oversight of Jack Smith specifically, tying his firing directly to his association with the Trump prosecutions rather than to any identified performance or misconduct issue

The normal administrative check on such a firing -- appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board -- was unavailable because the board itself had been left without a quorum by a separate Trump personnel action

offense_category: Statutory Violation — Commemorative Works Act (40 U.S.C. §§8901-8909) and 40 U.S.C. §8106 (unauthorized construction of a monument on federal land in the National Capital area) — NOT charged; this is a planning/permitting-stage dispute, not yet a completed unauthorized construction, and is most likely to be resolved via litigation or congressional action rather than criminal process
incident_summary: The Interior Department, under Burgum, has proceeded with planning and environmental review (Section 106 Assessment) for a 'Triumphal Arch' monument at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C. -- nicknamed the 'Arch de Trump' by critics -- despite the Commemorative Works Act requiring specific congressional authorization for any new memorial on federal land in the capital, which Congress has not provided for this project. Senate and House committee ranking members, citing their own Congressional Research Service analysis, formally notified Burgum and NPS officials that the project lacks the legal authorization the Act requires.
elements_required: Commemorative Works Act requires congressional authorization, via specific enacted law, before a new commemorative work may be placed on federal land in the National Capital region (40 U.S.C. §8902(a)(2))
No such congressional authorization has been enacted for this specific project
Interior/NPS proceeded with planning, environmental review, and permitting processes for the project despite the absence of authorization
Separate violation alleged under 40 U.S.C. §8106 (a related capital-construction statute)

evidence.description: Senate and House committee ranking members with jurisdiction over D.C. monument construction sent a formal letter to Burgum and NPS officials stating that Congress has enacted no law authorizing the Arch, and that Congressional Research Service analysis requested in January reached the same conclusion -- that absent such authorization, the project would not comport with the Commemorative Works Act
evidence.maps_to_element: No congressional authorization exists; CRS (a nonpartisan body) independently reached the same legal conclusion

evidence.description: The letter notes that since 1986, every memorial placed on federal land in the capital under the Act -- more than forty in total -- has gone through Congress first, with the World War II Memorial alone requiring two separate acts of Congress before NPS issued a construction permit, establishing the project departs from uniform historical practice
evidence.maps_to_element: Pattern evidence establishing the authorization requirement is consistently enforced for comparable projects

evidence.description: Interior/NPS proceeded with a formal Section 106 Assessment of Effects Report and draft Programmatic Agreement for the project, indicating substantive agency action toward construction despite the documented authorization gap

evidence.description: The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts approved the arch's concept design in April 2026 (dropping four lion sculptures originally planned for its base), and in July 2026 the National Capital Planning Commission voted 8-1 to approve the project with possible modifications, following a meeting with three hours of public comment that was almost entirely opposed to the arch; final NCPC approval is set for September 2026
evidence.maps_to_element: Documents the project advancing through two major federal design-review approvals despite the documented Commemorative Works Act authorization gap -- strengthens the 'proceeded despite the defect' element

evidence.description: A group of veterans and a historian filed a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration seeking to block construction, arguing among other grounds that the 250-foot arch would disrupt the sightline between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House at Arlington National Cemetery; six lawmakers (five representatives, one senator) separately sent a formal letter stating Interior and NPS have 'no power to build' the arch without congressional approval, citing both the Commemorative Works Act and the Height of Buildings Act given the arch's 250-foot height
evidence.maps_to_element: The litigation this entry previously said had not yet been filed now exists; also identifies a second, independent statutory objection (Height of Buildings Act) beyond the Commemorative Works Act question

Chutkan told DOJ's counsel at the hearing she did not want to 'wake up' to bulldozers at Memorial Circle while the case remained pending. This ruling predates and was never incorporated into this entry's prior updates.

A CRS analysis -- nonpartisan, written for Congress, not an advocacy document -- concluded this is a violation. Interior hasn't countered that analysis; it's kept proceeding.
cause: Documented in congressional oversight letters and budget comparisons: Interior is advancing a presidentially-favored monument through executive permitting and environmental-review processes in the same budget cycle where National Park Service maintenance budgets face proposed cuts of up to 40 percent. That's not a coincidental parallel -- it's a documented resource prioritization choice that reflects which projects the administration is willing to advance through informal executive processes versus which need statutory authorization. incident_summary: In November 2025, The Washington Post reported the Coast Guard would no longer classify swastikas and nooses as hate symbols under a new workplace-harassment policy, instead labeling them merely 'potentially divisive.' Kevin Lunday's order to maintain the hate-symbol classification was never actually incorporated into the policy for reasons that remain unclear, and the more lenient 'potentially divisive' language was allowed to take effect in mid-December 2025 despite objections from members of Congress. Facing renewed uproar, the Coast Guard deleted the downgraded language again on December 18, 2025, restoring the hate-symbol classification for a second time. offense_category: Defiance of a Federal Court Order -- Terminating a Union Contract Hours After a Judge Ordered Its Reinstatement -- a district court's contempt inquiry, not yet a finding; VA disputes the characterization
incident_summary: In August 2025, the VA canceled its collective bargaining agreement covering roughly 320,000 employees, implementing Trump's executive order stripping collective bargaining rights from large parts of the federal workforce on stated national-security grounds. The employees' union sued, and on March 13, 2026, a federal judge (a Biden appointee) ordered the VA to reinstate the bargaining agreement, finding VA had improperly canceled it as retaliation for the union's opposition to administration policies and had provided no evidence supporting its claimed national-security rationale. Just hours after that ruling, the VA filed an after-hours court notice re-terminating the same union contract -- conduct Government Executive characterized as drawing a judicial rebuke for 'blatant disrespect.' The judge gave the administration until the following Tuesday to explain why she should not hold VA in contempt of her March 13 order, and scheduled a contempt hearing for April 3, 2026. Government Executive later reported this was VA's third attempt to scrap the same union contract, with the dispute continuing to return to court in the months that followed.

VA's re-termination of the same contract occurred within hours of that order, via an after-hours court filing rather than through any new factual or legal basis addressing the court's findings
The judge's original ruling found VA had provided no evidence for its stated national-security justification, meaning the re-termination was not accompanied by newly cured evidentiary support
The judge treated the timing and manner of the re-termination as serious enough to initiate a formal contempt inquiry, not merely to note continued legal disagreement

incident_summary: In April 2026, a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of North Carolina indicted former FBI Director James Comey over an Instagram post depicting seashells arranged on a beach to spell '86 47,' which prosecutors characterized as a threat against President Trump. This is a legally separate indictment from the 'lying to Congress' case this tracker already documents (prosecution/cabinet-level/halligan-comey-vindictive-prosecution-2025-2026.json), which was brought in the Eastern District of Virginia by Lindsey Halligan and dismissed in November 2025 after a court found Halligan's appointment unlawful; the two cases share only their target and their connection to the broader pattern of prosecutions against Comey. In late May 2026, Matthew Petracca, the lone prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina assigned to the seashells case, withdrew without public explanation; DOJ filed a notice replacing him with Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy Severo. Comey's legal team has moved to dismiss the case on selective- and vindictive-prosecution grounds and separately argues the seashell image does not meet the legal standard for a 'true threat.' Comey has also alleged in a July 2026 court filing that the Secret Service illegally surveilled him in connection with the case. The case is set for trial in October 2026 after Judge Louise Wood Flanagan granted a defense request to delay proceedings.

official: Darin Smith, Interim/Confirmed U.S. Attorney for the District of Wyoming
offense_category: Prosecutorial Misconduct Before a Grand Jury -- calling defendants 'murderers' to grand jurors, telling them deliberations 'won't take long,' and engaging in off-the-record conversations with jurors during breaks between indictments
incident_summary: On May 15, 2026, three federal judges in the U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming jointly dismissed felony grand jury indictments against nine defendants -- Cheyenne Swett, Richard Allen, Michael Scott Hopper, Brian Joseph Johnson, Dennison Jay Antelope, Mathew Christopher Jacoby, Matthew Miller Jr., Wolf Elkins Duran, and Jose Benito Ocon -- citing 'deeply concerning' misconduct by then-interim U.S. Attorney Darin Smith. The judges found Smith called defendants 'murderers' to the grand jury, told jurors deliberations 'won't take long,' and had improper off-the-record conversations with jurors during breaks between indictments, writing that 'this misconduct began with some of the first words spoken to the grand jury' and calling it 'one of the few rare cases that rises to the level of dismissal.' The indictments, which included a murder charge, were dismissed without prejudice, allowing the U.S. Attorney's office to re-present the cases to a new grand jury. Despite these findings, the U.S. Senate confirmed Smith as Wyoming's permanent U.S. Attorney days later.

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Gutting Internal Civil Rights and Detention Oversight Offices While Immigration Enforcement Expands -- eliminating the internal check mechanisms specifically designed to catch abuse in the enforcement activity documented elsewhere in this tracker
incident_summary: DHS purged staffing at its Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties by roughly 85% and cut the Immigration Detention Ombudsman's office -- which investigates complaints about conditions and treatment in ICE detention -- by more than 90%, according to Mother Jones' reporting. These are DHS's own internal oversight mechanisms, specifically created to catch and address civil-rights violations and detention-condition abuses within the department's own operations, distinct from external oversight bodies like the Inspector General or Congress. The staffing cuts leave ICE's rapidly expanding detention and enforcement operations -- documented elsewhere in this tracker, including the AP's review of ICE employee misconduct (ice-misconduct-oversight-weakened-2026.json) -- with substantially diminished internal capacity to receive, investigate, and act on civil-rights and detention-condition complaints. This February 2026 report is itself an update on a story that began nearly a year earlier: DHS issued Reduction-in-Force notices in March 2025 that would have eliminated nearly all staff at these same three offices (Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, and the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman), prompting an April 2025 lawsuit from Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, the Southern Border Communities Coalition, and the Urban Justice Center. incident_summary: In late January 2025, a longtime DHS staffer -- who had worked at the department in various roles since the George W. Bush administration, including through Trump's first term -- accidentally added a journalist to a group email containing unclassified but sensitive details (timing and possible target-home addresses) about an upcoming ICE operation in the Denver area. She caught the error immediately, contacted the journalist, who agreed not to publish, and the operation proceeded without incident. Despite causing no operational harm, DHS placed her on administrative leave, opened an internal investigation, asked her to take a polygraph and surrender her cellphone (she declined both), and moved to revoke her security clearance -- a step that could end her career -- giving her 30 days to appeal. NBC News reported the story March 27, 2025, explicitly framing it as raising questions about unequal punishment for inadvertent leakers under the Trump administration. Hegseth faced no discipline, criminal charge, or removal; the Pentagon Inspector General's eventual December 2025 final report (tracked separately in this database, see hegseth-signal-yemen-strike-2025-03.json) found DoD Instruction and Federal Records Act violations but no referral for prosecution.

incident_summary: DHS created a public website in December 2025 branding a list of roughly 25,000 arrested immigrants as the 'worst of the worst,' which Secretary Noem, DHS, and the White House heavily promoted on social media to justify the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement operations. A CNN analysis found the site's crime descriptions were riddled with errors, with hundreds of individuals' listed charges misrepresenting the severity of their actual offenses -- for example, minor offenses characterized in ways suggesting serious criminality. After CNN presented its findings, a DHS spokesperson admitted the charges against hundreds of listed immigrants had been described incorrectly, attributing the errors to a 'glitch' the agency said it worked to fix, and the agency updated the site the same week. John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under the Obama administration, said the vast majority of so-called 'criminal aliens' are actually people charged with or convicted of traffic offenses, DUIs, and immigration-related offenses -- not violent or serious crime.

Legal scholars and critics quoted across multiple outlets characterized the arguments as 'built on a racist foundation.' If the Supreme Court adopts the administration's interpretation and reverses the long-settled reading of the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause, legal experts warned it could render hundreds of thousands of children born in the U.S. to immigrant parents stateless.

A federal magistrate judge rejected Peters's bid for release on bond in December 2025, and she remained in state prison. incident_summary: A whistleblower, represented by Whistleblower Aid, first raised a concern with the Intelligence Community Inspector General (ICIG) in May 2025 and in June 2025 requested the disclosure be transmitted to Congress; the complaint alleges that Gabbard's ODNI general counsel failed to report a potential crime to the Department of Justice. The complaint and an underlying classified intelligence report were not provided to the congressional intelligence committees until February 3, 2026 -- nearly eight months later -- when the ICIG's office finally handed it to the Gang of Eight lawmakers because of its classified contents. Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chair Mark Warner and House Intelligence Committee Ranking Member Jim Himes publicly demanded answers from Gabbard about the delay. Gabbard denied any wrongdoing, calling claims that she or ODNI 'hid' the complaint 'a blatant lie'; the ICIG's office separately stated it found the underlying allegation against Gabbard not credible and that the eight-month delay was justified. Congressional Republicans on the relevant committees rejected the complaint's substance, while Democrats continued to press over the length of the delay itself, a separate question from the complaint's underlying merits. comeback: There's a meaningful difference between 'finding a different legal basis for a policy goal' and 'achieving substantially the same outcome the Supreme Court just said exceeded the President's authority, using a different procedural label.' Greer's own public statement is the best evidence against this defense: 'the policy hasn't changed, just the legal playbook.' That's not a statement about adapting to a legal ruling -- it's a direct admission that the goal was continuity of the invalidated program. An administration genuinely responsive to a Supreme Court ruling reconsiders the scope of what it's doing; an administration that just swaps statutes while keeping the policy identical is treating the Court's ruling as a procedural inconvenience, not a substantive limit. The Section 301 workaround faces its own legal challenges for the same underlying reason -- Congress appears to have intended it for one country at a time, not blanket global tariff programs -- which, if correct, would make this a second episode of the same pattern.
cause: Consistent with patterns elsewhere in this dataset (Vought's impoundment strategy, the broader IEEPA/Section 122 sequence), this reflects a documented administration approach of treating adverse legal rulings as obstacles to route around via alternative statutory mechanisms rather than as binding determinations of the limits of executive authority. Cross-cutting pattern worth noting in debate: this is the same strategic posture documented in the Vought entry (act first, let legality get litigated afterward) applied to trade policy.

official: Lindsey Halligan, Interim U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia (appointment found unlawful by a federal court)
offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) and unlawful interim appointment (violated the 120-day limit on serving without Senate confirmation) -- the underlying charges against James Comey were brought and then dismissed; Halligan herself has not been personally charged with anything
incident_summary: In September 2025, President Trump forced Erik Siebert, then-U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, to resign after Siebert concluded there was insufficient evidence to charge former FBI Director James Comey with lying to Congress ('He didn't quit, I fired him!' Trump wrote on social media afterward). Siebert's deputy, Maya Song, was demoted and later pushed out of the department entirely. Trump then installed Lindsey Halligan -- a former personal attorney to Trump with no prior prosecutorial experience -- as interim U.S. Attorney, and Halligan personally secured indictments against both Comey and, separately, New York Attorney General Letitia James. In November 2025, Judge Cameron Currie dismissed both indictments, ruling that Halligan's appointment had violated the 120-day limit for serving as interim U.S. Attorney without Senate confirmation, and that all actions flowing from her defective appointment -- including securing and signing Comey's indictment -- were unlawful exercises of executive power that had to be set aside. DOJ appealed and, as of February 2026, continued to defend Halligan's appointment; a separate January 2026 judicial order required Halligan to explain why she was still describing herself as U.S. Attorney despite the ruling against her. Beyond the dismissed case itself, the push to prosecute Comey destabilized the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia: more than a half-dozen career prosecutors were demoted or pushed out amid the fallout, other prosecutors left voluntarily rather than risk being assigned to cases they viewed as improper, unrelated major prosecutions (including a terrorism case tied to an attack in Afghanistan) were disrupted by the turmoil, and after the district's judges unanimously selected a new U.S. Attorney to replace Halligan, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche fired that judicially-selected replacement, leaving the office without settled leadership for months.
elements_required: A career prosecutor (Siebert) with direct knowledge of the case's evidentiary strength was removed specifically after concluding charges were not supportable, rather than for an unrelated performance reason
His replacement (Halligan) had no prior prosecutorial experience and a documented personal/political tie to the President (former personal attorney)
A federal court found the replacement's appointment itself legally invalid, and voided every prosecutorial action she took as a result, including the indictment
The case targeted a prominent, named Trump critic (Comey) over conduct tied to a matter of long-standing presidential grievance (Comey's role in the Russia-interference investigation era)
Institutional damage extended well beyond the single case -- mass prosecutor departures, a disrupted unrelated terrorism prosecution, and repeated leadership churn in the same office

incident_summary: On April 2, 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth forced Gen. Randy George, the Army's 41st Chief of Staff, into immediate retirement -- roughly a year and a half before the end of his traditional four-year term -- and fired two additional senior Army generals the same day: Maj. Gen. William Green Jr., the Army's chief of chaplains, and Gen. David Hodne, commander of Army Transformation and Training Command. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell announced George's departure as effective immediately. Lt. Gen. Christopher LaNeve, recently sworn in as the Army's vice chief of staff, was reported as the likely successor; LaNeve had previously served as a military aide to Hegseth personally. The removals occurred during the active U.S. war with Iran and extend a broader pattern of Hegseth removing senior military leadership across the armed forces, documented separately in this tracker (kacher-joint-staff-removal-2026.json, an earlier Joint Staff Director removal). Update: The Washington Post reported that Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said he had no plans to resign following clashes with Hegseth in the aftermath of the George/Hodne/Green removals and continued reports of dysfunction inside the Pentagon; the White House publicly backed Driscoll even as tensions with Hegseth continued. official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (with President Trump as the removing authority)
offense_category: Politicized Removal of the Joint Chiefs Chairman, Chief of Naval Operations, and Three Service Judge Advocates General Without Stated Cause -- the JAG removals specifically raise a contested statutory concern under the law protecting judge advocates' independent legal advice function
incident_summary: On the night of Friday, February 21, 2025, the Trump administration fired Gen. CQ Brown Jr., Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and only the second Black officer to hold the post; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, Chief of Naval Operations and the first woman to hold that role; and Gen. Jim Slife, Air Force Vice Chief of Staff -- the first time in U.S. history two sitting members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff had been removed simultaneously. The same night, the administration also fired the Judge Advocates General (the top uniformed lawyers) of the Army, Navy, and Air Force -- Lt. Gen. Joseph Berger (Army), Rear Adm. Lia Reynolds, acting Navy JAG, and Lt. Gen. Charles Plummer (Air Force) -- a set of firings legal commentators dubbed the 'Friday Night Massacre of Judge Advocates General.' No public, on-record reason was given for any of the removals. Hegseth announced Trump intended to nominate retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Dan Caine as the new Joint Chiefs chairman. Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, characterized the firings as 'part of a broader, premeditated campaign by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth to purge talented officers for politically charged reasons,' a characterization widely connected in contemporaneous and later reporting -- including The Guardian's March 15, 2025 retrospective on Hegseth's broader reshaping of the Pentagon -- to the administration's stated opposition to diversity, equity, and inclusion policies and to Hegseth's public, pre-confirmation criticism of Brown's and Franchetti's selection. This entry documents the origin point of a pattern this tracker separately documents continuing into 2026 through the removal of Vice Adm. Fred Kacher as Director of the Joint Staff (kacher-joint-staff-removal-2026.json), the forced retirement of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George (hegseth-army-chief-staff-purge-2026.json), and Hegseth's later interventions blocking promotions of Black and female officers (hegseth-promotions-blocked-2026.json).
elements_required: 10 U.S.C. provisions governing the Judge Advocates General prohibit any DoD officer or employee from interfering with a TJAG's ability to give independent legal advice to the service Secretary or Chief of Staff, or with any judge advocate's ability to give independent legal advice to commanders -- [contested application, not adjudicated] removing all three service JAGs simultaneously, without stated cause, is argued by legal commentators (Lawfare, Justia/Verdict) to functionally undermine this independent-advice protection, though the statute does not clearly specify removal procedure and the administration's Article II removal authority over these positions is itself a live legal question, not settled

The Joint Chiefs Chairman and service-chief removals themselves fall within the President's broad Article II authority to remove senior military leadership and are not, on their own, alleged to violate a specific statute -- the accountability concern here is the documented pattern and stated politicized motive, not an established legal violation for those two removals specifically

incident_summary: On March 1, 2026, an Iranian one-way attack drone struck a tactical operations center at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, killing six soldiers of the U.S. Army's 103rd Sustainment Command and wounding more than 20 others. The Washington Post, based on interviews with 17 soldiers and other witnesses, reported that commanders had received repeated, specific warnings before the attack that the facility was highly vulnerable to drone strikes, and ignored them. Survivors told CBS News the facility's defenses -- T-walls designed to stop mortar and rocket fragments, not aerial drone strikes, with vertical blast barricades but no overhead protection -- were essentially nonexistent against the actual threat: one survivor rated the position's drone-specific defense as 'none.' Survivors also said the unit had been positioned within Iranian missile and drone range even as other units in the area were relocated, and that after the strike, senior officers abandoned the building rather than organizing aid for the wounded, leaving triage disorganized amid chaotic, severe injuries (perforated eardrums, heavy bleeding, head wounds). Secretary Hegseth publicly described the attacking drone as a 'squirter' that penetrated the defenses of a 'fortified' position -- a characterization survivors directly dispute, with one soldier stating: 'Painting a picture that 'one squeaked through' is a falsehood. I want people to know the unit was unprepared to provide any defense for itself.' Soldiers who were present say they fear no one will be held accountable for the command decisions that left them exposed.

incident_summary: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth personally removed nine officers from a list of 22 selected for promotion to one-star admiral, a list that had been approved by a board of senior Navy admirals through the Navy's standard vetting process. Three of the nine officers removed are women and two are Black men. incident_summary: When the U.S. began bombing Iran on February 28, 2026, roughly half a dozen U.S. Merchant Marine Academy cadets were aboard five privately-owned, U.S.-flagged vessels in the Persian Gulf as part of their required sea-training program. Declassification authority is not the same as operational security authority -- he had the legal right to decide what was classified, not the right to send strike timing over his personal phone outside secure channels. Citing a win on one question to dismiss a loss on the other is the kind of sleight-of-hand a genuinely strong position shouldn't need.

offense_category: DOJ Investigation of the Opposing Party's Fundraising Infrastructure, Directed by Presidential Memorandum and Escalated by Parallel Congressional Contempt Proceedings -- an institutional-accountability claim about coordinated multi-branch pressure on a single-party target, not a criminal charge against any named official
incident_summary: The congressional side of this effort began even earlier than the DOJ probe: by March 27, 2025, congressional Republicans and Elon Musk were already targeting ActBlue with investigations and subpoenas, with lawmakers requesting the Treasury Department turn over 'suspicious activity reports' involving the platform, and Musk accusing ActBlue -- without evidence -- of 'supporting' street protests and vandalism. In April 2025, President Trump signed a memorandum directing then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate online political fundraising platforms for alleged straw-donor and foreign-contribution violations; although the memo nominally covered 'other online fundraising platforms' as well, ActBlue -- the Democratic Party's dominant fundraising platform, which has processed nearly $17 billion in donations since 2004 -- was the only platform named. ActBlue called the memo a 'brazen attack on democracy in America.' In parallel, House Republicans led by Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan, Oversight Chair James Comer, and House Administration Chair Bryan Steil pursued their own year-plus congressional investigation into ActBlue's foreign-donation vetting practices. An April 2, 2026 New York Times report cited internal ActBlue documents describing the resignation of interim general counsel Aaron Ting and an internal message from former legal counsel Zain Ahmad alleging retaliation after he reported misconduct internally -- documents the House committees said ActBlue had not produced despite subpoenas. On June 10, 2026, ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones invoked her Fifth Amendment right more than 20 times during a House Administration Committee hearing, declining to answer questions about foreign-donation vetting and the exodus of ActBlue's legal and compliance team. On June 22, 2026, the three House chairmen sent ActBlue a formal letter stating the platform had withheld 422 requested documents under an attorney-client-privilege claim the committees rejected as baseless, giving ActBlue until June 26, 2026 to comply or face a contempt-of-Congress referral -- explicitly run in parallel with, and citing, the DOJ investigation Trump had directed over a year earlier.

incident_summary: ICE and CBP added roughly 920,000-995,000 DNA profiles to the FBI's Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) in 2025 alone, making DHS the single largest source of new genetic profiles in the database -- over 3.3 million profiles by December 2025, per Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology and WIRED's joint investigation. incident_summary: An Associated Press review found at least two dozen ICE employees and contractors have been charged with crimes since 2020, involving patterns of physical and sexual abuse, corruption, and other misuse of authority. incident_summary: ICE agents attempted to pull over a van in Newark, New Jersey on February 25, 2026; when the driver fled, agents pursued, and the chase ended in a multi-vehicle crash at Clinton Avenue and 10th Street. Newark police were not involved in the pursuit and responded only to the resulting crash. Newark Mayor Ras Baraka publicly said ICE failed to follow New Jersey's vehicle pursuit guidelines and called for accountability. In response, Baraka signed an executive order barring immigration enforcement operations in Newark city buildings without a judicial warrant and directing city employees to report suspected unauthorized federal enforcement activity.

Local police were not involved in and did not authorize the pursuit, indicating it was conducted under federal rather than coordinated local authority

official: Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary (Kristi Noem held the role and publicly defended the enforcement framing described below through her March 2026 removal; Mullin was Senate-confirmed 54-45 on March 24, 2026 and sworn in effective March 31, 2026)
offense_category: Sustained Public Mischaracterization of ICE Enforcement as Targeting 'Criminal Aliens'/'The Worst of the Worst,' Contradicted by the Administration's Own Internal and Reported Data -- an institutional-accountability and public-transparency claim, not a criminal charge against Noem personally; attributed to her as DHS Secretary with operational oversight of ICE, per this tracker's institutional-attribution standard
incident_summary: Beginning within Trump's first two weeks back in office, reporting repeatedly found that ICE's actual enforcement and detention activity did not match the administration's public framing that enforcement prioritized 'criminal aliens' and 'the worst of the worst.' HuffPost reported in early February 2025 that nearly half of those arrested or deported had no criminal record beyond immigration violations, and that ICE raids and deportation flights (including to Colombia) swept up children and pregnant women alongside anyone undocumented, following new Trump orders that eliminated prior, narrower enforcement priorities. In June 2025, CNN reported that internal ICE data it had obtained showed fewer than 1 in 10 immigrants detained since the prior October had been convicted of serious crimes like murder or assault, with over 75% having no criminal convictions beyond immigration or traffic violations. In July 2025, a CBS News analysis found that after Trump's daily deportation target jumped to 3,000 in May 2025, arrests of immigrants with no criminal record surged more than 250%, with only about 8% of all detainees having any violent-crime conviction. This pattern predates and is distinct from a later, separate entry in this database documenting a specific December 2025 DHS 'worst of the worst' public website found to contain factual errors overstating individual arrestees' offense severity.
elements_required: The administration's public messaging, from the first weeks of the term onward, characterized ICE enforcement as targeting convicted criminals and 'the worst of the worst'

The Department of Defense defended the hire, stating Irizarry was 'a qualified, patriotic young professional,' despite reported concerns raised internally by Pentagon officials about the appointment.

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Whistleblower Protection Act / First Amendment Retaliation Against Federal Employees -- NOT charged criminally; challenged via a federal civil lawsuit and Office of Special Counsel complaints, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: On September 4, 2025, two former senior NIH officials -- Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID, the position Dr. Anthony Fauci previously held), and Dr. Kathleen Neuzil, former director of NIH's Fogarty International Center -- filed a joint whistleblower complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel alleging they were forced out of their positions in retaliation for objecting to the cancellation of research grants and clinical trials, the politicization of scientific decisions, and what they described as baseless hostility toward vaccines from newly installed NIH leadership. Marrazzo, who had been placed on indefinite leave in March 2025, alleged Principal Deputy NIAID Director Dr. Matthew Memoli made statements mirroring Kennedy's views that 'vaccines are unnecessary if populations are healthy' and that NIH 'should not focus on vaccines.' Neuzil, placed on administrative leave April 12, 2025 before involuntarily resigning, separately objected to NIH canceling grants based on what she called 'anti-South Africa hostility' and an incorrect belief that certain grants advanced diversity, equity, and inclusion goals. Both officials' complaint also alleged that a $500 million universal-flu-vaccine program NIH awarded in May 2025 bypassed normal scientific peer review despite relying on technology multiple scientists described as badly outdated. Twenty-two days after filing the OSC complaint, on September 26, 2025, Secretary Kennedy fired Marrazzo outright. Marrazzo subsequently sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, naming Kennedy, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, Memoli, and NIH as defendants, alleging the termination violated the Fifth Amendment's due process guarantee, the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, the Administrative Procedure Act, the First Amendment, and the Whistleblower Protection Act.
elements_required: A federal employee engaged in protected whistleblowing activity (filing an OSC complaint alleging agency wrongdoing)
The employee's supervising official had knowledge of the protected activity
An adverse employment action (termination) followed the protected activity within a timeframe supporting an inference of retaliation
The stated agency rationale for the action does not independently account for the timing or the specific retaliatory statements alleged

evidence.description: Marrazzo and Neuzil's joint September 4, 2025 whistleblower disclosure to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel, alleging retaliation for objecting to grant/clinical-trial cancellations, vaccine-hostile statements from NIH leadership including Dr. Matthew Memoli, and a $500 million flu-vaccine program that bypassed normal peer review

evidence.maps_to_element: Adverse employment action following protected activity, with timing supporting a retaliation inference

official: Kelly Loeffler, Administrator of the Small Business Administration
offense_category: Hatch Act Violation (5 U.S.C. §7323, prohibiting partisan political activity by federal employees using official resources) — NOT charged criminally, addressed via Office of Special Counsel complaint process; this entry has stronger documentary evidence (cited internal emails) than the parallel Turner/HUD entry in this dataset
incident_summary: During the 2025 federal government shutdown, SBA's Chief Human Capital Officer sent internal emails (dated September 30 and October 1, 2025) instructing SBA employees to post partisan political messaging on official agency channels -- including the agency website, district office voicemails, and out-of-office auto-replies -- blaming one political party for the shutdown. A House committee letter to Loeffler cited these specific internal emails and characterized the conduct as 'a gross misuse of federal resources and a betrayal of public trust,' separately noting career civil servants do not swear their oath to a political party. Public Citizen also filed a Hatch Act complaint against Loeffler personally alleging she engaged in 'electioneering' while on duty during the same shutdown period.

The internal email evidence is what makes this entry stronger than the parallel Turner/HUD entry: directing career civil servants to post explicitly partisan framing on official agency channels, voicemails, and auto-replies via formal written instruction from the Chief Human Capital Officer is different in kind from an individual official making a statement. official: Linda McMahon, Secretary of Education
offense_category: Unauthorized Transfer of Congressionally Mandated Programs (potential separation-of-powers/ultra vires violation -- the Department of Education was created by Congress via the Department of Education Organization Act of 1979, and the statutes governing the transferred programs were separately enacted by Congress) — NOT criminally charged; addressed via formal impeachment articles (procedural, not expected to succeed given Republican control of both chambers) and ongoing political/legal dispute, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: Beginning May 2025, McMahon approved a series of interagency agreements transferring the administration of more than 100-140 programs and services -- governed by statutes including the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, Higher Education Act, Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act, Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, and civil rights enforcement under the Civil Rights Act, Title IX, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, and the Age Discrimination Act -- to the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, Justice, State, and Interior, without congressional authorization. House Democrats, led by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, filed articles of impeachment in June 2026 alleging these transfers violated federal law and that McMahon made false and misleading statements to Congress about them.
elements_required: The Department of Education and the programs in question were established and assigned to that Department by specific acts of Congress
Congress has not separately authorized the transfer of these programs to other departments
Documented, dated approvals of interagency agreements effecting the transfers

Whether 'interagency agreement' authority can lawfully accomplish what would otherwise require congressional action is the central legal question -- a genuine, unresolved point of administrative law, not a settled violation

evidence.description: McMahon approved a documented sequence of interagency agreements on specific dates: May 21, 2025 (Perkins Act programs to Labor), September 30, 2025 (ESEA and Higher Education Act programs to Labor), February 20 and 23, 2026 (additional ESEA/HEA programs to HHS and State), and June 15-16, 2026 (IDEA and civil rights enforcement under five separate statutes to HHS and DOJ)

evidence.maps_to_element: Direct testimony confirming the transfers and the resulting reduction in enforcement capacity

official: Chad Mizelle, former DOJ Chief of Staff and senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi
offense_category: Public Solicitation of Politically-Screened Hiring for Career (Nonpartisan) Federal Prosecutor Positions -- assistant U.S. attorneys are, by law and longstanding DOJ practice, career civil-service positions meant to be filled and evaluated apolitically, distinct from the political appointees at DOJ leadership
incident_summary: In early February 2026, Chad Mizelle -- former DOJ chief of staff and a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi -- publicly called for lawyers who 'support President Trump' to apply for career federal prosecutor positions, suggesting he could help such applicants secure the jobs. Assistant U.S. attorneys, who investigate and prosecute federal cases, are supposed to be nonpolitical and nonpartisan career civil servants, distinct from DOJ's political-appointee leadership. About forty minutes after Mizelle's post, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller amplified it, adding 'Patriots needed.' The call came amid mounting DOJ turmoil over politically charged personnel decisions, including the firing of prosecutors and investigators connected to earlier Trump-related cases and the pursuit of investigations against several of the President's political opponents. A former federal prosecutor quoted in ABC News's reporting warned that explicitly recruiting career prosecutors on the basis of political loyalty could be 'dangerous' to the office's traditional independence. That call was followed by a concrete policy change: MS NOW (Rachel Maddow Show) reported DOJ began waiving standard experience requirements for new federal prosecutor hires, allowing some candidates straight out of law school to be hired, amid widespread career-prosecutor departures and reported difficulty recruiting qualified replacements given the loyalty-test dynamic Mizelle's post captured.
elements_required: A senior former DOJ official with a continuing advisory role to the sitting Attorney General publicly solicited applicants for career (not political-appointee) federal prosecutor positions using explicit political-loyalty language ('support President Trump')
A senior White House official amplified the same call using similarly loyalty-coded language ('Patriots needed') within the same hour
Assistant U.S. attorney positions are, by design and longstanding DOJ norm, meant to be filled and evaluated on professional merit rather than political allegiance

The call occurred amid documented, separate instances of DOJ personnel actions against career staff connected to Trump-related investigations, providing context for concern that political-loyalty screening was already an operative practice, not merely rhetorical

evidence.description: In a July 27, 2026 statement to Raw Story, DHS moved further, stating in writing: 'ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.' This is DHS's clearest statement to date that ICE does not intend to target polling places, but it preserves the same threat-based exception Mullin described in June, which voting-rights advocates have characterized as vague enough to function as a loophole for a pretextual 'threat.'

status: As of this update, DHS's position has evolved from Mullin's March 2026 flat refusal to rule out ICE presence at polls to a narrower, conditional formulation: Mullin said on June 14, 2026 that ICE would deploy 'only' in response to a 'threat' (e.g., a bomb threat), and DHS put a similar position in writing to Raw Story on July 27, 2026 -- 'ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations' but may make arrests at a polling location as the result of a 'targeted enforcement action' tied to an 'active public safety threat.' No completed deployment of ICE to a polling place has been identified as of this update, and no unconditional written non-deployment commitment of the kind state election officials originally requested has been given -- DHS's own language keeps a threat-based exception open. No new deployment has occurred; this remains a documented pattern of conditional, narrowing-but-incomplete assurances rather than either a completed violation or a clean resolution.

State election administrators aren't asking for a policy philosophy -- they're asking for an operational assurance they can plan around, and the refusal to provide it is itself the documented concern. Worth keeping this entry framed carefully in debate as 'a documented refusal to provide the standard written assurance that federal law enforcement won't be used to chill voter participation' -- not as 'ICE went to the polls,' which would be inaccurate and easily rebutted.

The more defensible framing: an administration that has used immigration enforcement in an expanding set of public venues (courthouses, churches, schools, airports during funding lapses) in ways courts have repeatedly found legally questionable, and that has declined to draw a bright line excluding polling places. Whether this reflects a deliberate incremental-expansion strategy or ad hoc enforcement overreach is genuinely uncertain, and should be presented that way in debate.

Best used in debate as 'DHS has repeatedly declined to give an unconditional non-deployment commitment, offering instead a narrowing series of threat-based carve-outs that critics say could be used pretextually' -- not as 'DHS deployed agents to polling places,' which has not happened.

official: Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Misuse of a Federal Database / Unverified Public Claims Undermining Election Confidence -- DHS urged states to purge voter rolls using a system built for benefits-eligibility screening, not citizenship verification, after removing the system's own accuracy disclaimer, based on an unverified 250,000-noncitizen figure -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin urged state election officials to 'scrub' voter rolls using the expanded SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) system, claiming 250,000 noncitizens are registered to vote across four states -- California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Nevada -- without explaining how DHS verified that figure. SAVE was originally built to verify eligibility for government benefits, not to confirm citizenship for voter-registration purposes; the Trump administration expanded the system in 2025 to query voter registration data nationally using Social Security numbers and demographic information. A USCIS fact sheet that had acknowledged SAVE 'may not be able to confirm U.S. citizenship for individuals not designated as citizens in SSA records' was subsequently removed from public view. The Social Security Administration itself has said its citizenship data provides only 'a snapshot,' not 'definitive information about citizenship status,' and a 2006 federal audit found SSA had misclassified 3.3 million U.S. citizens as noncitizens, with 7% of people SSA flagged as noncitizens turning out to be eligible voters. Utah's own comprehensive SAVE-based review flagged 9,000 voters as potential noncitizens, but manual review found more than 5,600 of them were, in fact, U.S. citizens -- a majority-error rate. Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar called DHS's 250,000 figure 'wildly speculative at best,' and voting rights experts characterized the underlying data process as 'garbage in, garbage out.' Former Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson separately warned about SAVE's accuracy based on county registrars' experience obtaining citizenship documentation that contradicted SAVE's flags. Update 2026-08-18: the same July 17, 2026 announcement in which Mullin made the 250,000-noncitizen claim and sent the four states' letters also included, at a same-day press conference, explicit threats that noncompliant election officials could face 'fines, ... penalties, and even, depending on how far it goes, prison time,' and that noncompliant states could lose federal election-security grant funding -- a materially more coercive characterization than 'urged,' corroborated across ABC News, Common Dreams, and States Newsroom/Herald and News coverage of the same speech and letters.

The system used (SAVE) was designed and built for a different purpose (benefits eligibility) than the one it is now being used for (citizenship/voter-roll verification)
DHS or USCIS removed its own prior public disclaimer about the system's reliability limitations for this use case
Independent, real-world application of the same system (Utah's review) produced a documented, high error rate flagging actual citizens as noncitizens

official: Elon Musk, former DOGE leader / Special Government Employee
offense_category: Evasion of Court-Ordered Testimony Regarding DOGE's Dismantlement of Federal Agencies -- a civil-litigation accountability claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: Beginning in mid-November 2025, constables and private process servers made repeated attempts -- including at least four separate attempts at Musk's Brownsville, Texas property near SpaceX headquarters, and at his West Lake Hills, Texas residence -- to serve Musk with a subpoena for deposition testimony regarding his role in DOGE's dismantlement of federal agencies, including USAID. Process servers were repeatedly denied entry to gated properties, and staff told servers Musk was not home and no one was authorized to accept paperwork on his behalf. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang ruled in early February 2026 that Musk and State Department officials must sit for depositions regarding USAID's dismantlement, rejecting a motion for a protective order that argued the testimony was barred by protections for high-ranking officials. The Justice Department intervened on Musk's behalf in the litigation. On March 4, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled 2-1 to grant Musk's petition, blocking the deposition from proceeding. As of CNN's April 13, 2026 reporting, the underlying question of whether Musk would ever be compelled to testify about his DOGE role remained unresolved, with appeals and higher-court rulings having stalled the process for more than a year since the litigation began.

The Justice Department intervened in the litigation in a manner that supported Musk's position rather than remaining neutral
An appellate court ultimately blocked the deposition on a divided 2-1 vote, and more than a year after the litigation began, no deposition had occurred

offense_category: Misuse of Administrative Subpoena Power to Target Protected Speech -- no criminal charge; this is a First Amendment/investigative-power-abuse accountability claim, distinguished from a judicial subpoena because administrative subpoenas require no judge's approval
incident_summary: A Washington Post investigation found DHS used administrative subpoenas -- which, unlike grand jury or judicial subpoenas, require no judge's sign-off -- to obtain personal data on government critics and people engaged in constitutionally protected speech, including at least one case in which DHS sought to identify a person who had emailed a DHS attorney criticizing the agency's handling of an asylum seeker's case. The ACLU separately moved to quash a DHS administrative subpoena it characterized as aimed at tracking down a man who had criticized the department. Following the Post's reporting, a bipartisan group of three Democratic and three Republican lawmakers, led by Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Adriano Espaillat, introduced the Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act, which would require government officials to certify under penalty of perjury that they are not using subpoenas to monitor or retaliate against people exercising free-speech or other constitutionally protected activity, and would separately limit the government's ability to obtain phone records without a judge's order.
elements_required: DHS used administrative subpoenas -- issued without judicial approval -- to obtain personal identifying data on individuals whose only documented connection to any DHS matter was criticizing the agency or a specific case, not any alleged unlawful conduct

At least one specific, named instance is documented (the individual who emailed a DHS attorney with criticism) and a second is independently corroborated by the ACLU's own motion to quash a similar subpoena
The response to this pattern was bipartisan, not partisan criticism -- three Republican and three Democratic members of Congress co-sponsored corrective legislation specifically citing this conduct

Secretary Noem, as the DHS official ultimately accountable for the department's use of its subpoena authority, is the accountable official, whether or not she personally authorized each individual subpoena

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security (fired March 2026, reassigned to a newly created envoy role) / Corey Lewandowski, senior DHS adviser
offense_category: Retaliatory Personnel Practices and Contracting Centralization Producing Documented Dysfunction Across a Cabinet Department -- distinct from this tracker's other DHS entries (subpoena abuse, surveillance audit), which concern specific external-facing actions rather than internal management conduct
incident_summary: A Wall Street Journal investigation found significant infighting, dysfunction, and self-promotion-driven decision-making at the top of DHS under Secretary Kristi Noem. Roughly 80% of ICE's career leadership was fired or demoted during Noem's tenure, with the Journal reporting career immigration-enforcement staff were let go or demoted specifically for questioning or objecting to Noem's decisions -- creating what multiple sources described as a culture of fear across DHS's 23 sub-agencies as Noem and senior adviser Corey Lewandowski fired, reassigned, and demoted personnel. The Journal also reported Noem tracked border czar Tom Homan's television appearances to ensure she received more airtime than him, despite the two rarely speaking directly. Separately, Noem and Lewandowski centralized control over DHS contracting, which the Journal reported led to delays, higher prices, and potential conflicts of interest. Noem was subsequently fired as DHS Secretary in March 2026 and reassigned to a newly created envoy role.

The scale is substantial and specific: roughly 80% of ICE's career leadership fired or demoted, not an isolated personnel dispute

Contracting authority was centralized in a manner the Journal's reporting connects to concrete negative outcomes (delays, higher prices, potential conflicts of interest), not merely a management-style preference
The dysfunction was severe enough that Noem herself was ultimately removed from the DHS Secretary role, an outcome indicating the administration's own leadership found the situation unsustainable

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Public Accusation of Criminal Assault via Official Social Media Without Charges or Convictions -- disproportionately targeting U.S. citizens; not a criminal charge against Noem herself, a due-process/accountability claim regarding DHS's public communications practices
incident_summary: A Wall Street Journal investigation reviewed more than 100,000 posts made over roughly a year by accounts linked to DHS, ICE, CBP, and senior administration officials including Secretary Noem, who was directly involved in publicizing the accusations as part of the administration's social-media campaign defending aggressive immigration enforcement. The Journal identified 279 people publicly accused by name or identifying detail of assaulting federal immigration or Border Patrol agents. Of those 279, 181 -- about 65% -- were U.S. citizens, not the undocumented immigrants the enforcement campaign is officially aimed at. The Journal tracked each identified case through the legal system: close to half of the 181 citizens accused were never charged at all, and none of the 279 total individuals identified across the full dataset had been convicted at trial as of the investigation's publication. The Journal's team separately reviewed more than 200 videos tied to the assault allegations, using both agency body-camera footage and bystander recordings, and found many of the videos cast doubt on the government's own claims that agents had been assaulted.

A majority (181 of 279, ~65%) of those publicly accused were U.S. citizens rather than the undocumented population the enforcement campaign is officially targeted at
Close to half of the accused citizens were never criminally charged, and none of the 279 total accused had been convicted at trial as of the investigation
Independent video review of over 200 incidents found many recordings cast doubt on the underlying assault claims themselves, not merely on whether charges were later pursued

White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller responded to case failures in Los Angeles by describing them on X as 'mass judge and jury nullification... of slam-dunk assault cases against federal law enforcement,' while the National Lawyers Guild characterized Section 111 as 'the Government's Offense of Choice' for silencing dissent toward immigration operations

offense_category: Perjury / Knowingly False Statements to Congress -- Noem was referred for investigation, not charged; DHS denies the allegations, so this is a contested referral, not an adjudicated violation
incident_summary: On March 16, 2026, Senate Judiciary Whip Dick Durbin and House Judiciary/Oversight Democrats, led by Rep. Jamie Raskin, formally referred Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem to the Department of Justice for investigation into potential perjury and knowingly false statements to Congress, based on her testimony before House and Senate committees on March 3 and 4, 2026. The referral identified four categories of allegedly false statements: (1) Noem claimed DHS had not violated any court orders, when in fact DHS had repeatedly defied court orders to release individuals from ICE detention, in some cases failing to release people for days or weeks after a court-ordered release date; (2) she made claims about the bidding process for a $220 million DHS television ad campaign contract that the referral disputes; (3) she made claims about the detention of U.S. citizens by immigration agents, despite ProPublica having separately documented more than 170 U.S. citizens held by immigration agents; and (4) she made claims about detention conditions. A DHS spokesperson responded that 'any claim that Secretary Noem committed perjury is categorically FALSE.' A congressional criminal referral does not compel DOJ to open an investigation, and DOJ -- under the same administration Noem serves -- was not reported to have opened one as of this entry's sourcing.

The referral was made through a formal, bipartisan-eligible congressional channel (Judiciary Committee leadership in both chambers) rather than informal criticism

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Suppressing an Inspector General Finding to Evade a Statutory Deadline, Then Giving Congress a Contradicted Sworn Account of Compliance
incident_summary: In July 2025, DHS ended the requirement in place since 2006 that airline passengers remove their shoes during TSA security screening. A classified DHS Inspector General report completed in November 2025, based on undercover 'red team' testing, found that many of the full-body scanners used at TSA checkpoints cannot effectively detect threats concealed in shoes -- meaning the policy change created a documented new security vulnerability. The Inspector General's office alerted Secretary Noem's office to the finding in August 2025. Rather than taking public or substantive corrective action, Noem's DHS reclassified the report, elevating it and limiting its release, despite a statutory requirement that the department address the issue by January 30, 2026. In subsequent sworn testimony to lawmakers, Noem stated that 'all of the recommendations' in the Inspector General's report had already been implemented. A March 4, 2026 memo from Inspector General Joseph Cuffari's office stated it had not received any evidence supporting that claim. Sen. Tammy Duckworth formally demanded DHS rescind the 'shoes on' policy, citing the watchdog's finding that it 'created a new security vulnerability.'
elements_required: A classified Inspector General report, based on documented red-team testing, found a specific, concrete security vulnerability created by a policy Noem's DHS enacted
DHS was subject to a statutory deadline (January 30, 2026) to address the finding and did not take substantive corrective action by that date
DHS instead elevated the report's classification, an action that limited its release rather than addressing the underlying finding

offense_category: Firing the Nation's Top Signals-Intelligence and Military Cyber Officials Based on an Outside Activist's Personal Loyalty Test, Leaving the NSA and Cyber Command Without Senate-Confirmed Leadership for Nearly a Year
incident_summary: On April 3-4, 2025, President Trump fired Gen.
